cards.title: Papyrus Sallier III
cards.text: An Egyptian poem about Qadesh presents Ramesses II as the hero. The copy lets us examine how that account presents him.
cards.limits: The account does not tell us how everyone on either side understood the battle.

cards.title: The Qadesh peace treaty and its replica
cards.text: Ramesses II and Hattusili III made a later peace agreement. The United Nations display is a modern replica of a clay record from Hattusa.
cards.limits: The later agreement cannot tell us who won the earlier battle.

cards.title: Turin Strike Papyrus
cards.text: Amunnakht recorded work stoppages near Deir el-Medina over missing provisions. His account includes a payment and later protests.
cards.limits: This is a scribe’s record of the dispute, not an interview with every worker or household.

cards.title: Turin Mine Map
cards.text: The map shows routes through Wadi Hammamat and uses different colours for different rock. The museum associates much of the writing with Amunnakht.
cards.limits: A record of roads and rock does not guarantee that a route is safe, open or best for everyone.

cards.title: Shelf-top route trial
cards.text: In Imani’s model, the short ridge path drops a tall crate. The wider wash takes two extra turns but keeps it upright. The ridge still works for a hand courier.
cards.limits: These are outcomes in a model, not ancient road measurements.

cards.title: The Singapore Stone
cards.text: An inscribed slab once stood by the mouth of the Singapore River. After its destruction, a surviving fragment eventually returned from Calcutta, now Kolkata, on indefinite loan.
cards.limits: The fragment preserves marks without giving us an agreed full reading. It cannot identify itself as the rock in a story.

cards.title: Badang and the rock
cards.text: The Sejarah Melayu, or Malay Annals, tells of Badang throwing a rock to the river mouth. In 1834, Peter James Begbie identified the thrown rock with the inscribed slab.
cards.limits: The story gives the rock meaning. The episode does not describe an inscription, so it does not identify the surviving object on its own.

cards.title: Receiving tag signed by Ketta
cards.text: The archive worker Ketta signed the line marked “received at the hall”. A second line for the maker is blank.
cards.limits: The signature records a handover. It cannot tell us who made the tag or whether Ketta used the stamp first.

cards.title: Cloth from the keepers’ practice table
cards.text: The keepers practiced the crossed mark on scrap cloth before stamping their own tags. Leila now shows new keepers where to leave room for a second name.
cards.limits: Leila can show how keepers use the mark here. She cannot identify who made the loose hall tag.

threads.title: The Workmen’s Thread

nodes.label: The first stoppage
nodes.text: Amunnakht records a crew stopping work and asking for provisions. Start there: who is speaking, and who is writing?

nodes.label: A payment
nodes.text: A later entry records a grain delivery. Grain was part of the crew’s regular provisions. Lay a marker for that delivery.

nodes.label: The workers return to protest
nodes.text: The scribe records a further stoppage after the grain delivery. Keep both marks in order. The record still shows a dispute after the payment.

gap.text: The record brings us close to the workers’ demands. It cannot tell us what each household thought or how every family got by.

threads.limit: This thread follows entries in one administrative account. Repeated entries are not independent witnesses.

labelKits.title: The two dates at Qadesh
labelKits.oldLabel: The treaty proves who won the battle.

A later agreement between two rulers

weak.noSupport: A visitor carries away the word “proved”. By the next shelf it has turned into “everyone agreed”.
weak.tooStrong: Someone repeats only your largest claim. The second date drops out.

Badang’s rock in the Malay Annals

weak.tooStrong: “Settled,” a visitor repeats. The part about the evidence disappears.

weak.noSupport: A visitor calls the person on the tag its maker. The gold edge shows that a receiving line cannot carry that claim.
weak.tooStrong: The word “first” sticks in a reader’s ear. The room starts to glow.

legends.subject: Record on the stand
legends.criterion: What a reader can carry away

characters.name: Nasir
characters.role: Keeper of the archive copies; fictional

characters.name: Leila
characters.role: Keeper of the workers’ reading room; fictional

characters.name: Marek
characters.role: Keeper of the route model; fictional

characters.name: Nellis Haig
characters.role: A runner hired by the Gilded Seal

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: I heard the latch from across the hall. Elsbet put three records behind this door. Someone has set out a notice calling them all proof of the same thing.

options.text: What did Elsbet leave behind?
I’ll start with the royal records.
I’ll speak to the people tending the records.
Who made the crossed mark on the hall tag?

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: A narrow strip of paper. No date, just a sentence in her hand: “Read the back before you carry the front into town.” I thought she meant a page.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: Nasir’s room lies north. There is a poem beside a later treaty. The labels keep sliding together, as if the dates can be rubbed out.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: Take the west door for the workmen’s record. Or follow the east passage to the route model. The attendants have been waiting for someone who asks before they announce.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: The Nexus is about to open this exhibit to visitors. Work two leads before you decide what we send back. The third will still be here when you return.

dialogue.speaker: nile-nasir
dialogue.text: I nearly put the treaty under the poem. It looked so tidy. Then I put the Lens on the dates.

options.text: What should I look for?
Build a label people can repeat.
I’ll look at the two cases.
Move the seal to what the desk checked.

dialogue.speaker: nile-nasir
dialogue.text: Start with the two cases. Look once at what happened and once at when someone made the record. Either object can take the first line, if the words fit it. Once you have the dates, turn over the brass seal between the cases. My desk left a check on its back.

dialogue.speaker: nile-nasir
dialogue.text: I left a space between the cases. A visitor can cross it in one step. The Lens makes the years harder to skip.

options.text: Return to the label stand.
Leave the hall.
Move the seal to what the desk checked.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: There’s grain listed on the page. A visitor saw that line and said the workers went back happy. Walk the three stops before you tell me what you hear.

options.text: Whose record is it?
I’ll follow the thread.
Ask how the papyrus names the person who recorded the dispute.
Read the workmen’s room slip.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: The museum identifies the scribe as Amunnakht. We can listen closely to the demands he records without claiming we heard every person in the village.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: The grain entry shows when provisions came. The later stoppage shows that the dispute was still open. I’ll keep both slips together. Which one should face the corridor?

options.text: Lead with the workers stopping work. Put the payment and renewed protest beside it.
Lead with the payment. Put the later protest in the next line so payment doesn’t sound like a settlement.
Keep the slips open. I want to examine the papyrus first.
Ask how the papyrus names the person who recorded the dispute.
Read the workmen’s room slip.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: That puts the workers at the entrance to their own story. I’ll move the official reply alongside, where it can answer them. Leila sets a narrow paper window over your first slip. A visitor reads the stoppage and asks how the people in charge replied. Two readers left notes marked “Closed” on the exit peg. Turn the slips over to see what each reader means.

options.text: Leave the opening slip in place.
Turn the clips with the same reading window.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: The official reply can go first, if the next line keeps the dispute open. I’ll pin both slips under the same clip. Leila sets a narrow paper window over your first slip. A visitor reads that grain arrives and asks if that settled the matter. Two readers left notes marked “Closed” on the exit peg. Turn the slips over to see what each reader means.

options.text: Leave the opening slip in place.
Turn the clips with the same reading window.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: Two folded reading slips hang from the peg. Both have CLOSED on the front. Each points to the grain delivery in Amunnakht’s account.

options.text: Turn over the stock keeper’s slip.
Turn over the lending bench slip.
Lay both slips beside the later stoppage.
Read the stock keeper’s posted note.
Read the lending bench’s posted note.
Leave the slips on the peg.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: There is a single box next to the delivery line. At our stock desk an apprentice learns to close the entry when the delivery goes in the book. Another box can open the next day. The slip only says that this delivery was entered.

options.text: Put the slip back with its box showing.
Leave the slips on the peg.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: There are two blank spaces for voices. At our lending bench the older readers teach each pair a closing call. The first voice says what the people asked for. The second says how the dispute ended. On this slip the second reader has used the grain delivery as the ending.

options.text: Put the slip back with both voices showing.
Leave the slips on the peg.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: The grain delivery appears in the source. The later stoppage appears there too. Perhaps the delivery answered the first request and a further demand brought the workers back. Perhaps people still wanted something the delivery left open. These three entries show work stopped again. They leave how each worker understood the payment open.

options.text: Pin a “Delivery entered” note by the exit.
Leave a second voice open at the lending bench.
Keep the slips together for now.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: A keeper copies “Grain delivery entered. Later stoppage recorded.” onto the corridor note. The next apprentice starts a fresh entry at the line about the renewed protest.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: Two readers take turns. One reads the grain delivery. The other goes to close the story, then sees the later stoppage. She passes the slip back to the first reader and asks what the record can tell them about the new stoppage.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: The clips have stopped rattling. People pause over the second slip now, long enough to see why the first one cannot stand alone.

options.text: Leave the room open.
Try the two readings again.
Try the two readings again.
Ask how the papyrus names the person who recorded the dispute.
Read the workmen’s room slip.

dialogue.speaker: nile-marek
dialogue.text: I built two roads on this table. Imani says the real map is waiting on the wall. I can rebuild a model in the morning; I can’t rebuild a source in the afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: nile-marek
dialogue.text: The Mine Map gave us the idea for two routes, not the numbers. The shelf-top model is beside you. Keep the load the same while you test both roads.

options.text: Leave the cart ready.
Try the tilt tray before we turn the cart.
Check what the museum links to Amunnakht on the map.
Read the Map Room slip.

dialogue.speaker: nile-marek
dialogue.text: Your delivery tag is already on the hook. If you want to see either run again, the model stays on the bench.

options.text: Leave the cart ready.
Try the tilt tray with the spare test block.
Check what the museum links to Amunnakht on the map.
Read the Map Room slip.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: The narrow rail has two fixed pins and a lower stop. Imani lays out two practice copies of the same size, cut from one sheet of card and based on Ketta’s receiving tag. Both show two circles. A porter said either one would hang. Check both against this rack.

options.text: Set the carrier’s punched copy against the stop.
Set the reading room’s printed copy against the same stop.
Leave the rail clear.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: Held against the same stop, only the punched copy went down over both pins. The circles match in place. The opening through the paper makes the difference on this rail. A receiving tag can sit ready for a carrier. The flat copy can help a reader follow its lines.

options.text: Put the punched handling copy on the rail.
Put the printed guide and original’s case number in the low tray.
Leave both copies at the testing rack.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: One packet fits the door before the hall opens. Imani sets down three address ties. “The street can read a short correction as it goes by. At the staffed table somebody can ask who wrote a slip. In the workshop somebody can try a load. I can open one of those places now. Who should get the morning?”

options.text: Send a two-date label to the public case.
Send the workmen’s two slips to the reading table.
Send the route trial and map to the workshop table, side by side.
Give me time for the third lead.
Check the folded packet’s two dates.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: Imani keeps the old claim where an early visitor can read the crossed-out words. She puts the two dates beside it. “They can check what we changed before anyone arrives to explain why. I’ll have to tell the people waiting for the table.”

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: Imani takes two stools to the reading table. “They can hear which grain payment the scribe recorded, and ask who never got to speak. A visitor who has to keep walking will see an empty case.” She sets one stool low enough for a child.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: Imani has one hand on the model when the door starts to close. “The apprentice gets a morning to try the load. Put the ancient map beside it with its own date. The model can answer a question about weight. It cannot tell us who made that journey.” Behind her someone folds up the public reading stand.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: Your first packet has gone. Use the Door Without a Name to follow it, or stay to trace the lead you left. Neither choice shuts the archive.

options.text: Where did a reader send a reply?
Put our paired copy to work.
Where did a reader send a reply?
Put our paired copy to work.
Where did a reader send a reply?
Put our paired copy to work.
Leave the archive open.
Check the visitor’s link between two records named for Amunnakht.
Bring the two keepers’ notes to the filing desk.
See the cross-index the readers used.
See the two-room reading slips again.
Check the folded packet’s two dates.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: Imani lays out a practice packet. Both date slips say First Bell. A visitor read them as the same day. Line up the torn edge and the two punched holes before we use either slip.

options.text: Fit the sending stub to the torn flap.
Fit the shelving slip to the torn flap.
Clip both fitted slips beside the flap to compare them.
Leave both slips on Imani’s desk.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: Day 4 on the sending stub. Day 5 on the shelving slip. The tear and holes join them to the same practice packet. The dates tell when it left the shelf and when a reader could open it. We have no stamp for the crossing time. Where should the next visitor find this check?

options.text: Mount both dates beside the Nexus case for walk-up readers.
Keep the signed shelving slip at the staffed pickup desk.
Leave both slips on Imani’s desk.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: The torn corner and both holes line up. The sending stub has the packer’s mark and says Day 4, First Bell. Our packing crew calls the date at handoff. The next crew uses it to find the bundle that left their shelf.

options.text: Return the stub to the folding desk.
Set the sample down.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: The shelving slip fits the second edge and has the same two holes. The Nexus keeper signed it Day 5, First Bell. Their trainees stamp the slip when a reader can open the copy.

options.text: Return the shelving slip to the folding desk.
Set the sample down.

dialogue.speaker: warden-ise
dialogue.text: I hoped you’d find Elsbet’s letter. She refused to name the room until she knew what belonged in it. Find the blue-and-brass door on the north wall of the east wing.

dialogue.speaker: warden-ise
dialogue.text: A visitor has crossed out “victory proved”. She’s still looking at both dates. Elsbet used to leave her corrections where the original readers could find them.

options.text: Clip the correction beside the old title.
I’ll come back.

dialogue.speaker: warden-ise
dialogue.text: The reading table filled before the main case did. One visitor asked which workers the scribe never heard. We’ve left a seat for that question.

options.text: Which slip are visitors reading first?
Lay both slips beside the reader’s seat.
I’ll come back.

dialogue.speaker: warden-ise
dialogue.text: An apprentice weighed the empty case before trying the model. Then he asked whether the cast could tell him anything the map could not.

options.text: Which delivery reached the table?
Leave the ancient route and the model side by side.
I’ll come back.

dialogue.speaker: warden-ise
dialogue.text: One last thing. You turned over the carrier. I can see where Elsbet scratched something out. Not the name of a place. A name of a person.

options.text: Tell me about the new return table.
I found where the seal stayed whole.
I’ll come back.
Unfold our working slip beside this packet.

dialogue.speaker: warden-ise
dialogue.text: The doors are staying open. A packet can change what people look at first. It cannot decide what they notice next.

options.text: What’s on the return table?
Which trail did I send?
Leave the case open.

dialogue.text: Two records from the Singapore River have arrived in the east wing: a stone fragment and a story. The person who set them out joined their labels with a single pin. See if it belongs there.
dialogue.speaker: warden-ise

dialogue.text: The case keeps the lead you chose. The other trails are still open behind the blue-and-brass door.
dialogue.speaker: warden-ise

dialogue.text: The carrier brought the map and trial notes. What it carried beside them depends on the tag you tied. The workshop kept the tag for anyone to read.
dialogue.speaker: warden-ise

dialogue.text: The first slip is the one you put facing the doorway. Look at the reading table after we open it. The second slip is still there.
dialogue.speaker: warden-ise
warden-ise
dialogue.text: Then the cut came from inside the archive. We can leave the porter’s name out of the search. I’ll start with the return slips, not the gate book.

dialogue.speaker: keeper-oduya
dialogue.text: Oduya pins a new strip beside the old sign. Now people who saw the original can follow the correction. A copy stays here, where a later reader can ask for both.

dialogue.speaker: keeper-oduya
dialogue.text: Oduya sends a copy to the market and asks the people who first carried the story to read it back. The people who aren’t there can still find the dated change on the old board.

dialogue.speaker: keeper-oduya
dialogue.text: We changed the sign on Corvan’s stall. We never told everybody who heard the old claim. You’ve seen a packet travel to different readers. How shall we carry a correction through town?

options.text: Hang a dated correction by the guild hall. The people who saw the old sign pass that door.
Ask the people who carried the old story to give the correction in their own words.
I’ll leave it on your desk for now.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: The visitor who copied the royal case sent a folded slip to Nasir. Find it by the cases. Follow his blue cord to the next test copy.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: Nasir sets the old heading under a hinge. At the case the visitor can lift it to check the dated correction. Someone with only the pocket copy still has to come back.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: Imani fills a tray in the hall. Visitors can take both dates home on each strip. A copy with the original heading stays in the Royal Records Room for anyone who wants to see what changed.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: The fold hid what the second date belonged to. We have two ways to send the paired headings back. What should Nasir set up first?

options.text: Hang a hinged copy on the royal case.
Send folded copies out with the two dates attached.
Leave both copies here for now.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: One of Leila’s readers carried the two slips into a family reading. Find her reply beside Leila. It marks the moment the second slip fell out of the telling.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: A family takes two seats in the Workmen’s Room and goes back to the second slip. The record stays open at its own pace. Visitors who never enter the room will have to hear of it from another reader.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: Two visitors take turns at the bench. One reads the payment, the other the next stoppage. The dated slips stay under their hands. Imani leaves a spare copy for visitors who want to read quietly.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: Leila has kept the scribe’s name with both lines. Do we put the passages where people can take their time or pass them between readers in the hall?

options.text: Keep the paired slips open at Leila’s table.
Put a two-reader copy at the hall bench.
Leave both copies here for now.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: An apprentice has sent Marek a copy of the workshop notes. See what came unstuck beside the model. Nasir has the next test copy in the Royal Records Room.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: Marek’s next apprentice reads the load settings before setting the cart on the shelf. The tag stays by the bench. A reader far from the model will need a copy.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: Nasir puts a copy in the Royal Records Room. Readers can trace the map separately from the model, even when the bench is busy. The ledger alone cannot give them the feel of a loaded cart.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: We can help visitors rebuild the trial or help later readers trace what was actually tested. Where should this copy do its first work?

options.text: Tie the run card and its settings to the model bench.
File the source and the run on facing pages.
Leave both copies here for now.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: People keep bringing me tags with Ketta’s name on both lines. The receiving tag is beside the old stand. Leila shows the apprentices how they make their marks in the Workmen’s Room.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: Under the same paper window, the same visitor now reads about the grain first. “Oh. So they paid and the workers stayed?” Lift the paper. The renewed stoppage is right where it was. You changed the opening and kept the window and the lines. You have heard what this reader made of the two openings.

options.text: Ask Leila how people carry these readings home.
Close the window for now.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: Under the same paper window, the same visitor now reads the stoppage first. “So the payment was one answer to a demand.” Lift the paper. The renewed stoppage is right where it was. You changed the opening and kept the window and the lines. You have heard what this reader made of the two openings.

options.text: Ask Leila how people carry these readings home.
Close the window for now.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: The visitors here have two habits. People who learned the stories at our lending table take turns speaking a request and then its reply. The desk readers start with the dated delivery line they can check in the book. When a paper leaves this room, it needs a name and a date for either reading. The source gives a record of more than one stoppage. It leaves the workers’ private feelings open.

options.text: Hang both ways of reading with names and dates.
Keep the reading window. Pin the full sequence below it.
Leave the slips as they were.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: Leila pins the lending-table reading beside the desk order with the scribe’s name on both. Two readers can hear the other order without swapping the source.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: Leila keeps the paper opening. Under the flap she pins the stoppage, payment and later stoppage in order. On the outer tab she names the two reading habits so a visitor can see why either might start somewhere else.

dialogue.speaker: nile-nasir
dialogue.text: A visitor saw the brass above the words “victory proved” and took it as my promise. My desk traced the copies. We can put that check where we can stand behind it. Each caption still needs its own record and date.

options.text: Move the seal to the catalogue desk.
Move the seal under the two separate copy labels.
Leave the seal loose for now.

dialogue.speaker: nile-nasir
dialogue.text: Nasir bolts the seal beside the catalogue check at his desk. The cases keep separate captions for the Egyptian account and the Hattusa treaty. A visitor follows a shelf number to ask what the brass mark covers before carrying the caption away.

dialogue.speaker: nile-nasir
dialogue.text: Nasir sets the brass low on a strip that only says “copies checked”. Both caption cards sit above it, each with its own date and source. A hurried reader can tell which description belongs to which case without walking to the desk.

dialogue.speaker: nile-marek
dialogue.text: An apprentice says the crate tipped because its contents shifted. This test crate is one solid block. Set it on the painted square with its broad side to the cord. Try it on the flat tray and on the same tray raised to the mark.

options.text: Set the tray level and let go of the block.
Raise the same tray to the mark and let go.
Pin a note from the two readings.
Leave the tray ready.

dialogue.speaker: nile-marek
dialogue.text: The solid block stays upright on the level tray. Chalk holds the starting square and the cord marks the same side of the block for the next reading.

options.text: Leave the tray for now.
Reset the tray for another reading.
Pin a note from the two readings.

dialogue.speaker: nile-marek
dialogue.text: The same solid block now tips at the marked raise. Nothing inside it can shift. The tray angle can account for a tip in this setup. A moving cart can also turn or jolt. Keep those as separate things to test.

options.text: Leave the tray for now.
Reset the tray for another reading.
Pin a note from the two readings.

dialogue.speaker: nile-marek
dialogue.text: Our two readings belong to the same tray, square and solid block. The ancient Turin Mine Map records routes. The slope mark on our tray comes from our trial. Where should the next keeper see that limit?

options.text: Carry the two settings to the cart bench.
Keep the trial limits beside the map case.
Leave both readings in reach.

dialogue.speaker: nile-marek
dialogue.text: Marek pins both readings and the starting square beside the cart. A keeper can repeat the tray test, then see where the cart adds motion and a turn.

dialogue.speaker: nile-marek
dialogue.text: Marek leaves a space between the map’s route caption and our two tray readings. A reader can follow the drawn route and still ask for a field reading before talking about its slope.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: A visitor clipped the Mine Map to the strike account under one name. They asked which road the workmen took when their grain ran short. The clip made two records look like one story. Read both of their dates, then ask Leila and Marek what their copy can tell us.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: The museum identifies Amunnakht as the scribe of this account. It records a stoppage, a delivery of grain and another protest. Year 29 belongs to the protest in the reign of Ramesses III. A reader can follow what the scribe recorded in that order. The line for the workers’ journey is still empty.

dialogue.speaker: nile-marek
dialogue.text: See how the date belongs to the map’s making. The catalogue associates much of its writing with Amunnakht. Keep the words ‘much of the writing’ with that link. We can point to roads and different rock colours in Wadi Hammamat. The workmen’s own route remains outside what this sheet can show.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: The strong lead is a name, but the two papers put it to different work. The strike account gives an order for events. The map lays out a place. We can let a reader find both records under a name, or send the two purposes back to the rooms as a pair of reading slips.

options.text: Add a cross-index under Amunnakht and keep a limit beside each entry.
Send one slip to each room that explains what its record can show.
Hold both copies here for a moment.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: A reader opens the index and puts a finger beside the map’s museum attribution. They can turn to either record. The separate entries give them a way to check which part of the link is an association.

dialogue.speaker: nile-iman
dialogue.text: Leila’s reader finds the protest dates at the workmen’s case. Marek’s reader finds the rock colours beside the map. I’ve put the other room’s name on the back of each slip so someone can still follow the link.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: Amunnakht’s account gives the order of the stoppage, payment and renewed protest. The date marks an event in the account. Turn over the slip for the Map Room and its separate source.

dialogue.speaker: nile-marek
dialogue.text: The mine map shows roads and rock. Its date concerns the making of the map. The museum links much of the writing to Amunnakht. The other side of the slip points to the separate workmen’s record.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: I left a practice slip pinned beside two lamp marks. A visitor counted two grooves and says a third was rubbed away. A reader says the third is shallow. The pins will keep the slip in place while you change the light.

options.text: Look down with the lamp above.
Move the lamp to the side.
Return the lamp above the same slip.
Set out the two readings together.
Read the desk guide again.
Read the paired lamp views again.
Leave the slip pinned down.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: Two grooves are clear from here. If a third were rubbed away, this view would look just the same. Change the lamp position and leave the pins alone.

options.text: Move the lamp to the side.
Leave the lamp above for now.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: A third groove comes into view at the edge of its shadow. The slip and pins stayed put. Move the lamp back to see whether the first view returns.

options.text: Return the lamp above the same slip.
Leave the lamp to the side for now.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: Two grooves show from above again. The angle changed what you could count. Favouring that explanation is abduction. The receiving team uses grooves to count boxes. We read aloud in turns here. I cut these to show where the next reader takes over. Keep that purpose beside the two views.

options.text: Leave a guide beside the lamp for readers who want to try it.
Send the paired view notes to the lending bench.
Leave the readings ready for later.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: A reader at the desk moves the lamp and sees the third groove return. The guide tells them where to put it back and why this particular slip carries pauses.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: Someone at the lending bench opens both views together. They can tell which lamp position produced each count. The note names this practice slip so the receiving team’s box counts stay in their own record.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Marek pinned a sketch of this room to a turning board. It says “Everyone turns left for the square,” and its key calls the square a display case. The Turin papyrus on the wall marks roads and rock in Wadi Hammamat. This sketch is ours. Try it where a reader enters and where a carrier sets down a box.

options.text: Hold the room marks steady and turn the sketch half a turn.
Set out the revised room guide.
Leave the sketch on the peg.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The arrow swung toward the crate rack. The case and rack stayed in place. Someone at the shelf mark can reach the case by turning right. The carrier’s square already meant the rack at handover. Marek’s square sent them to the place where readers look at the papyrus.

options.text: Set out the revised room guide.
Leave the sketch turned on the peg.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The large board can name landmarks that stay in the room. Small copies can give a left and a right from the exact point where someone starts. Give the case and rack their own marks and jobs. We can keep our room guide beside the old papyrus with its own name.

options.text: Put one guide on the board with both fixed landmarks.
Put a guide at each approach with its own directions.
Leave the two sketches together on the table.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: You clip a case symbol and a crate symbol to the board. Marek points out the two starting marks. A reader can follow the glass case. A carrier can check her box at the rack. The room guide stays separate from the papyrus on the wall.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: You clip the small guides at the aisle and shelf marks. Each starts with the place where it hangs. The two copies keep the same names for the case and rack. Marek puts a matching date on both so another keeper can replace them together.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: I deliver for the Seal. The receiving desk pays me for a signed arrival. This stamp says the file is complete too. If I go back with no stamp, a lamp may as well sign my wages. Leila left two clips on the workers’ copy. Let’s see what they do before we take the form apart.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: The grain arrived. The workers stopped again. I see why Leila left that second clip. My stamp joined up two jobs the same way. A public change needs a fresh signature and I miss my first slot. Fold it and I can make the slot, though most people at the stand will only read the outside.

options.text: Split the stamp line on the public docket.
Fold the open review beside the delivery receipt.
Leave the slip with Nellis and keep the stamp as it is.
I’ll come back to the stamp.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: Write my name on the delivery line. I’ll take that late slot. Leila can leave her check line where the next reader sees it. Keep a copy and bring it to the Cold Store.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: Leave “Review open” on the outside, please. My name can go inside the receipt. Put Leila’s two clips beside it. I can catch the first slot and you can bring a copy to the Cold Store.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: I’ll carry it the way they gave it to me. The receiver can still say what they signed for. If you come to the Cold Store, find me by the name rail.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: Read the docket by the stand. When the Cold Store opens, I’ll be there. You can check what came through with me.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: The next reader says someone pulled the guide away from its clip. They found it skewed after the door opened. The papyrus stays in its case. We can try the loose copy here and see what moves while nobody touches the rack.

options.text: Pin a folded strip by the guide’s corner.
Leave the loose guide on the rack.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: The corner lies against the fold. Stand at the quiet sill where the door and rack share a view. Leave the clip tight and keep the guide as it is.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: Take three beats from this sill. Keep the same guide, rack, strip and sightline. I can keep the door shut for one pass. When the hall is clear, I can open it once for the next pass.

options.text: Watch for three beats with the door shut.
Watch the same rack for three beats with one door opening.
Step away from the sill for now.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: Three beats pass. Nobody reaches the rack. Go back to the guide and check where its corner lies against the strip.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: The door swings. A loose thread at the edge of the rack rises. Nobody reaches the guide for those three beats. Go back to the same corner.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: The first corner stayed put. The second slid away with the open door. A hand could move the guide on another day. Today it moved while we kept that rack clear. The guide can stay where a reader expects, under clips. On the sheltered shelf it can lie loose, but we need a pointer.

options.text: Fit two spare clips to the entrance rack.
Move the guide to the sheltered shelf and leave a pointer.
Leave both observations with the guide.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: The guide stays at the entrance. A reader can lift a clip to turn a page. Keep my spare strip for the next place that needs to record what moved.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: The guide lies flat on the shelf with both readings beside it. The entrance arrow sends the next reader to it. Take my spare strip. A folded edge can hold a starting place elsewhere.

dialogue.speaker: nile-marek
dialogue.text: The receiver needs to move a teaching board at night. Leila’s readers need to follow marks to the edge of a broken source. Find their notes, the fragment in the Nexus and the map beside us. The museum map gives us named roads and rock colours. A stroke on the surviving stone can end at the break.

options.text: Put the support plan first and take the reading copy to Leila.
Put the two source tabs on the rail and give the receiver a separate board.
Leave both trays on the table.

dialogue.speaker: nile-marek
dialogue.text: I’ll leave a two-handled board in the hall. Its support line has its own space. Leila can give the class a lower copy in the Workmen’s Room. Go try both before a copy travels.

dialogue.speaker: nile-marek
dialogue.text: I’ll bring the stone tab and Mine Map key level with the reading rail. The receiver gets a separate small board in the hall. Check it on your way back so the receiver can find the handling line in the dark.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The old ticket says “the stone”. The night receiver reaches for the loose sheet. The cut board has two handles and a line for the edge of the teaching copy. Clip the ticket to the handles so it follows the board.

options.text: Seat the teaching copy on the board and lift it by the two handles.
Leave the copy on the table.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The board lifts and the loose paper stays flat. The receiver crosses out “the stone” on the ticket and calls for the teaching board. The name of the historical object stays on a source slip in its own pocket.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: A reader follows the road line in the map’s key. She moves the same tracing frame to the fragment and asks where to continue a stroke. Stop her frame at the broken edge. The copied trace can name the part she has in front of her.

options.text: Stop the tracing frame at the fragment edge and attach its source tab.
Leave the frame ready.

dialogue.speaker: nile-leila
dialogue.text: She moves her pencil along the marks and leaves the next space open. Someone can bring another reading to the same edge later. The map’s roads and rock colours can keep their separate key.

chronicle.title: First packet
chronicle.text: The public case keeps both dates in view.

chronicle.title: First packet
chronicle.text: The next reader hears the workers through a named record.

chronicle.title: First packet
chronicle.text: The workshop can compare a source with a trial.

chronicle.title: The Door Without a Name
chronicle.text: Elsbet left three records behind a door she refused to name. We crossed to the Nile archive to find out why.

chronicle.title: The crossed-out name
chronicle.text: The first packet is in use. Ise found a name beneath the carrier label. The archive is still open.

chronicle.title: One river, two records
chronicle.text: The return table now keeps the Singapore Stone fragment and the Badang account in view together, without using one to prove the other.

chronicle.title: A correction that travels
chronicle.text: Emberford placed the corrected claim where the people who met the old one can find it.

chronicle.title: A slip comes back
chronicle.text: A reader sent evidence that part of our first packet had come loose. We chose where to leave a paired copy.

chronicle.title: The borrowed mark
chronicle.text: The hall now leaves room for an unnamed maker alongside the record we can check.

questions.text: What changes when a record gives us the maker’s past, rather than the event itself?
questions.lastWord: A battle, its telling and a later agreement leave different dates.

questions.text: How does a sequence change what we think a source proves?
questions.lastWord: A payment and a later protest can both be true.

questions.text: What can a model let us decide, and where does that decision stop?
questions.lastWord: The route trial helps us make a choice inside the model.

questions.text: Who should hear an account first, and what changes with that choice?
questions.lastWord: Where the first packet goes changes who can use it.

questions.text: How do public corrections help people know what has changed?
questions.lastWord: A visible correction lets earlier readers see what changed.

questions.text: How can an account matter to a community when an object cannot verify every part of it?
questions.lastWord: A tradition and a fragment can each tell us something, without having to tell us the same thing.

questions.text: What must travel with a claim so it can be checked after it leaves its first reader?
questions.lastWord: Make the claim and its footing travel together.

hints.text: Elsbet’s letter points back to the Nexus.
Look along the North wall of the Nexus.
The Door Without a Name hangs beside the Hall of Firsts.
After reading Elsbet’s letter, use the door at the north side of the east wing.
The three rooms ask different things. Two will give you enough to send a packet.
Look for the Royal Records north of Imani, the Workmen’s Room west, or the Map Room east.
Finish a label, set the two workmen’s slips in order, or try both roads on the shelf-top model.
Complete any two activities. Return to Archivist Imani in the entrance hall.
Ask Imani about the folded packet after two inquiries.
Both desks used First Bell. Find the day on each slip.
Match the torn edge and two holes on both faces of the sample.
Fit the sending stub and the shelving slip. Read the different days and check what the two desks stamped.
Return to the folding desk after fitting both slips.
Decide how a visitor finds the signed shelving date.
The public clip is beside the east cases. The staffed copy is at the pickup desk in the east wing.
Follow your first dispatch back to the Nexus. Once it is on display, read the matching date clip or the signed desk receipt.
Try the small rail beside Imani.
Use its lower stop with each copy.
Check the result beside the rail each time.
Set the punched copy against the stop and check it. Set the printed copy against the same stop and check it.
Return to the rail after reading both results.
A carrier wants a copy that can hang. A reader wants a flat guide back to Ketta’s tag.
Put one of the copies where its reader can use it.
Mount the punched copy or set the printed guide in the low tray. Read the new check at its spot.
Imagine who opens the packet.
Which person would gain the most from the evidence you’ve worked with?
Speak to Imani at the entrance hall desk.
Choose one available destination. All supported choices earn equal credit.
The packet has crossed. Follow it.
Use the same door you entered through.
Ise is back at her desk in the main hall.
Talk to Warden Ise at her desk and carry out the action she offers.
Two cases tell two different stories.
The Date-Kind Lens can separate the dates.
Inspect Papyrus Sallier III and the treaty display. Use the Lens on both.
Draft a label about the poem’s account or the later agreement. Qualify it at the label stand.
A delivery is a point on the thread, not its end.
Inspect the Strike Papyrus in the west room first.
Follow the three thread points from left to right. Talk to Leila after the break in the thread.
Give either the stoppage or the payment the first line. Keep the later protest visible.
A map and a model answer different questions.
Look at the Mine Map in the east room. Marek built the model beside it.
Run the same cart on the ridge and the wash at the model. The delivery tags appear below the readings.
Read the Mine Map west of this model. Come back to the shelf to run the cart.
The ridge reading is saved. Choose “Run the cart on the wash” to add the other reading.
The wash reading is saved. Choose “Run the cart on the ridge” to add the other reading.
Both readings are recorded. Choose one delivery tag below them. The tags show what each delivery brings.
Choose “Run the cart on the ridge” and “Run the cart on the wash”. Then choose a delivery tag under the two readings.
Two records reached the same doorway.
Look near the east end of the Nexus hall.
Inspect the fragment on the east-wing bench and the Badang account beside it.
Use the Lens to separate the object’s recorded journey from the written identification.
A careful label leaves room for both kinds of record.
Try leading with the fragment or with the story, rather than proving they’re identical.
At the stand, pair the fragment with what survives, or Badang with how people remember the place.
Keep the limit about the uncertain link. Listen to what the visitor repeats.
A record travels back to the people it came from.
Return to the guild hall in Emberford.
Speak with Keeper Oduya about carrying a correction.
Use the option about Elsbet’s packet. Choose whether readers reach the correction in the square or hear it from someone first.
Someone carried the first packet away and sent a reply. Imani knows which keeper received it.
Ask Imani where the reader sent the reply. The keeper has left the reply with the record it refers to.
Read the slip from the public case in Nasir’s room, the reader’s ribbon in Leila’s room, or the apprentice’s loose tag beside Marek’s model, depending on your packet.
After reading that reply, follow its room clue. Inspect the two headings at Leila’s table, the reading clip beside Marek’s model, or the double clip near Nasir’s cases.
You have seen what can fall out of a copy. Imani can help you put the parts back in reach.
Return to Imani in the hall of the Nile Archive.
Tell Imani you want to put the paired copy to work.
Choose one of Imani’s two placements. The new prop appears where your choice sends it.
A name written on a tag may describe how the tag got here.
Look at Ketta’s receiving tag in the hall and the practice swatch in Leila’s Workmen’s Room.
See which line Ketta signed and watch what the swatch is for. The label stand is on the west side of the hall.
Mount a label about the handover or the practice and leave the first maker unnamed. Both displays can hold.
Leila keeps the slips in clips so the top line can change.
Speak to Leila in the Workmen’s Room after you choose which slip leads.
Turn the clips under the same paper window, then ask how the readers carry the story home.
Leave the readings side by side or keep the opening flap with the full record underneath.
A brass stamp can mark a very small check. Find out what this one covers.
Use the Lens on both cases in the Royal Records Room.
Turn the seal over between the two cases and use its backing to trace the display copies.
Tell Nasir to move the seal. Put the check at the desk or below the separate copy labels.
Marek has one test block and a tray beside the map.
After seeing the Mine Map, tell Marek you want to try the tilt tray.
Set the same block on the level tray and the raised tray. Keep the chalk square and cord fixed.
Pin the two readings beside the cart to let a keeper repeat the run, or beside the ancient map to keep the scope of the trial clear.
Find the two records that mention the scribe.
One date belongs to an event. Another dates the making of a record.
Visit the Workmen’s Room and Map Room. Inspect the Turin Strike Papyrus and the Turin Mine Map.
Use the Date-Kind Lens at both cases to keep their time claims separate.
Each archive keeper knows a different part of the file.
Start with the person who keeps the record you have just read.
Ask Leila about the workmen’s account. Ask Marek about the map’s attribution.
Use the new Amunnakht conversation choices in both rooms. Keep the map’s qualified link.
Choose where the next reader can use the notes.
The index connects two files. The room slips put a record’s purpose right beside it.
Return to Imani after hearing both keepers.
Choose an index or two slips. Keep both records and the different limits on what a reader may conclude.
A visitor and a reader disagree about a groove.
Find the pinned practice slip in the Workmen’s Room.
Move the lamp without moving the slip. Compare what you can see from above and the side.
Read the two grooves from above. Move the lamp to the side to reveal the third, then return the lamp above the slip.
Keep the lighting and the count together.
Leila’s pauses and the receiving team’s tallies serve different purposes.
Use the lamp’s note choices after you return it above the slip.
Leave a guide at the lamp for someone who can repeat it or a paired note at the lending bench for readers farther away.
Look for the two folded slips at the exit of the Workmen’s Room.
Look at the stock keeper’s box and the lending bench’s two voices. They both point to the delivery.
Lay both slips beside the later stoppage to see what each one leaves out.
Leave a dated sequence for the next apprentice or keep a voice open for the next pair at the bench.
The room sketch has a left arrow. The case cannot turn with it.
Try the aisle and shelf marks on opposite sides of Marek’s table.
Find the carrier’s check-in slip near the crates.
At the peg, turn the room sketch and see what the arrow points to.
The reader and the carrier need different stops.
Return to the turned sketch on the peg.
Choose a fixed landmark guide or a small copy for each starting point.
Read the guide on the peg or check both small copies where people approach the table.
One gold stamp reaches across two different jobs.
Nellis is by the delivery slip in the Nile Hall.
Read the stamp in the Hall and find Leila’s two clips in the Workmen’s Room.
See why the recorded grain delivery and the renewed stoppage keep two entries. Show what you found to Nellis.
The runner needs a receipt for a finished delivery.
Meet Nellis next to the stamped slip.
Choose what goes on the rail and in the travelling receipt, or leave the slip with Nellis.
Inspect the changed docket. The Cold Store gets its own copy when the runner moves on.
Someone found the guide out of place by the door.
Pin the folded strip near the guide in the Workmen’s Room.
Watch from the sill with the door shut. Return to its corner to see the first result.
Watch the same rack for three beats with one opening. Check the gap at the strip again.
Leila wants the guide to stay readable for the next visitor.
Talk through the clips by the rack once both watches are recorded.
Choose a clipped entrance guide or a sheltered shelf with a pointer.
Find the guide you left. Leila’s spare strip can travel to a second workshop.
A receiver and a reader need different things from the next case.
Find the receiver’s ticket in the Nile Hall and the reader’s note in the Workmen’s Room.
Inspect the Turin Mine Map here, then visit the Singapore Stone in the Nexus.
Use the two requests with the display trays at the back of the Map Room.
Two audiences can use the same source without following the same route.
Find Marek’s empty trays in the Map Room.
Choose the first display for careful handling or for close reading.
Go to the hall for the handling board. The reader’s frame will be at the Map Room rail or with Leila.
See what someone can do with each mount.
Use the two handles on the teaching board in the hall.
Find the tracing frame in the Workmen’s Room or Map Room, depending on what you put first.
Stop the frame at the broken edge. The finished copies can travel in two pockets.

journal.text: We brought a packet back to the Nexus. Its audience changed what they noticed first, without changing what the records could support.
At the Nexus return table we compared an artefact with a story of the same place. Both could have a place in the case without borrowing certainty from the other.
We carried an archive method back to Emberford. A dated correction belongs where the people who heard the first account can find it.
A reader showed us what our first packet lost on the way. We sent another copy with its headings, limits or settings still attached.
The name at the handover tells us who received the tag. The cloth shows how the keepers share a practice. Neither lets us sign the empty line.

journal.title: A name in two places
journal.text: The workmen’s papyrus records events. The Mine Map describes part of a place and links much of its writing to Amunnakht. The name helped me find two sources. I kept each claim with the record that could support it.

journal.title: The third groove
journal.text: The same practice slip showed two grooves from above and three when I moved the lamp to the side. Moving it back restored the first view. Leila’s marks tell a reader when to pause. The receiving desk uses its own cuts to count boxes.

journal.title: Two ways to close a slip
journal.text: I turned two slips that used the same word for different things. One marked a delivery entered in a book. The other tried to end a dispute. The later stoppage in Amunnakht’s record stays on the page either way.

The same landmarks fall on different sides when a reader turns around. A square at handover meant the crate rack. The room sketch used it for the glass case. We gave both destinations a name and left the roads and rock in Wadi Hammamat on the old map.

portfolio.title: Return to the Nexus and help Warden Ise put the packet to work.
portfolio.text: I helped open a public record and made a choice about who could use it first. I saw what happens when a record reaches a new audience.

clues.name: Elsbet’s unnamed tag
clues.text: Three holes held three cords. Someone cut them at the same length. The tag beneath has a trough where a word used to be.

views.text: Your seal fits the impression beneath the third cord. The cuts came afterward. Someone removed the labels without breaking the archive seal.
The key-plate has the same two screw marks. Elsbet moved this tag rather than scraping out the word where it hung. Look for who was meant to read it.

clues.name: The map’s margins
clues.text: The display case is empty beyond the ridge line. The margin is larger than you expected.

views.text: Kip’s map has an empty place too. His marks start where his feet have been. A blank patch is a boundary of the record, not a landscape without people.
Hesper checked a weight before she trusted the balance. Marek traced the same narrow turn at two cart widths before choosing the fixed one. Ask what the table does not vary.

clues.name: Your spare carrier tag
clues.text: Imani punched a second tag before the packet left. The place below the address is empty.

views.text: The graphite traces a little slot beneath the address, meant for a second reader. Elsbet left room for a later correction without scraping off the first record.

clues.name: Folded copy from the public case
clues.text: A visitor writes: “My fold covered the date on the agreement. At home I read it as part of the battle.” Nasir tied the fold shut with blue cord. A matching cord marks his dry run on Leila’s table in the Workmen’s Room.

clues.name: Two headings on one strip
clues.text: At Leila’s table, Nasir clips the date and the purpose together for each record. Fold either end back. Each visible heading still says which record it describes. Leila leaves enough room to pull the second heading out again.

clues.name: A reader’s ribbon
clues.text: A reader pinned a ribbon after the first grain payment. She writes: “I paused here. My brother thought the work was settled.” Leila sends you to Marek’s Map Room. He has built a holder that leaves space for a second line.

clues.name: Two places in a reading clip
clues.text: Beside the model, Marek slides the payment into one clip and the new stoppage into the next. Each clip carries its own speaker and date note. A listener can stop after the first line and still see that the second has a place.

clues.name: An apprentice’s loose tag
clues.text: The apprentice has copied “the wide wash kept the load upright”. The tag with the crate height fell out of the bundle. Marek ties it to his sample. Look for a double clip beside Nasir’s cases in the Royal Records Room.

clues.name: The double clip
clues.text: Nasir uses one clip for the map description and another for the trial result. Under the trial he leaves the load and road settings. A copyist can take the model note away and still see exactly which run produced it.

clues.name: The stamp’s backing slip
clues.text: Turn the seal over. Nasir’s mark links each display copy to a catalogue entry: the Egyptian papyrus gives a royal account of the battle; the clay treaty record from Hattusa records a later agreement. The United Nations keeps a modern replica of that clay record. A line through both catalogue entries reads “copy checked”. The larger heading above the seal reads “victory proved”. There is no check beside that heading.

keepsakes.name: A spare carrier rubbing
keepsakes.text: A graphite rubbing of the tag beneath Elsbet’s packet. It has space for a reply.
keepsakes.where: Follow a packet back to the Nexus.
keepsakes.use: Compare it with the spare carrier tag in Imani’s hall.

awards.name: The Record Travels
awards.earnedBy: You put the Nile packet to work at the Nexus.
awards.title: Keeper of Two Dates

memories.line: You found the unbroken seal. Good. I’d been ready to blame the porter.
Kip left the inland road blank. I like his map better for it.
A second reader. Elsbet always cut room for one more.
Two visitors came to my desk with the tag. This time they asked what Ketta received.
I left the spare cloth out. The new keepers are teaching the mark to each other.

items.name: Nellis’s carrier copy
items.description: The runner’s signed receipt from the Nile Archive. Its second line stays open for the separate check. Take the copy to Nellis at the Cold Store.

items.name: Folded witness strip
items.description: Leila folded this spare strip to hold a starting mark. Carry it to another bench and use the same fold to keep track of what moves or which count travels.

items.name: Two-pocket mount folio
items.description: Marek’s paired tabs for a teaching copy. One marks what you can move and where it starts. The other leads back to the documented object. Take the folio to the Trade Hall in the Metalworks.
